title: Hypothetical question: How would you feel if AI was used to make the game dynamically as you played it and it ran locally on your PC?
author: fatheadlifter
selftext:
AI has largely been used so far as a way to make offline content. Whether that's sprites (typically, common), 3D art (more recently), sound fx, voices or other stuff, typically it's been used for pre-generated content authoring.

Sometimes there's a game that runs in the cloud, or has a cloud backend component. Usually an LLM in order to generate some game dialogue or narrative bit. This has probably been the other major use case for AI in games so far, although this seems to be more the realm of indie dev and not the AAA's.

What happens when AI is essentially the game engine, and AI is making the game content as you play it? There have been some experiments in this direction, but just little demos that run in the cloud and not complete games.

And what if it didn't run in the cloud? It runs on your GPU locally, no internet required. AI is the engine, it's making unique content and an experience for you that's directed by a designer, but not sculpted or crafted in the traditional sense. It runs 100% locally on your PC, using your GPU.

I'm not going to predict when this shift in software development could happen, but it could happen one day and this idea would be different than all AI based games we've seen so far. If you hate this idea I'd like to hear why, or if you find this version of an AI game acceptable or even desired, I'd like to hear about that.

Looking for a civil discussion, honestly curious what you think either way.

comments.author: gcampos
comments.body: I would feel hot because every time my laptop runs a LLM for long, the fans goes to full speed

replies.author: fatheadlifter
replies.body: So the next-in-line concern becomes "it's going to make my GPU run too hot".  What if it didn't?  What if it was no more costly to run on your PC than any other game?

replies.author: -svde-
replies.body: concern, sure. that's why most don't go this route, because you can't control outside variables. do you have literally any idea how you would do that?

replies.author: fatheadlifter
replies.body: Well I'm an experienced game developer and I understand AI tech.  So I know where technology is at today broadly, I'm talking about a hypothetical type of game in the future.

replies.author: -svde-
replies.body: there is no telling what might happen with the progression of AI tech, and as the other commenter mentioned there are people already doing this plenty. it’s just doing it at scale .

comments.author: AlgaeNo3373
comments.body:
There's folks here in the sub already doing stuff like this, I'm one of them :)

"Local" can split into different things too. I recently learned via other prople's projects in this sub, that there are small models that ship with browsers (one with chrome, for example) that can drive a game, rather than cloud compute in the "rented server" sense. I like the use case personally. Has "edge computing" vibes or at least pushing in that direction - working with very little, optimizing, etc. Tends to be more lightweight than some might think when it comes to "AI powered".

replies.author: fatheadlifter
replies.body: I haven't seen any of those projects.  Every time I've looked at aigamedev I see the other use cases for AI in games, basically pre-authoring content and sometimes LLM use.  But maybe I haven't looked at the right times or just missed the good threads.

comments.author: LynxAfricaCan
comments.body:
I am heavy into AI from an enterprise/architecture/security perspective but not a game dev at all.

I think some things are a no brainer - AI should allow for fresh dialogue from NPCs for example. 

But if you are talking about a procedurally generated world that is being done by local llm? Or otherwise features/content that need to use the GPU at all?

That is taking resources away from running the actual game - id rather not have that and have better framerate, or have ray tracing on etc

The other aspect is quality. If you let AI create things on the fly without any feedback loop, all the guardrails/skills/prompt engineering in the world won't stop the weird hallucinations

Even in an entirely AI cycle, no humans in the loop - you need agents to check each others outputs

Some things would work well. NPC behaviour, dialogue, side quests, but even these are likely to be using cloud models

What do you really mean by "AI is the engine" ? I feel like this might be a misunderstanding of what AI , models, etc actually are - no offence

A model is just that - it's a probabilistic inference runtime. It takes inputs, generates outputs

You still need an engine/game/runtime/code of some sort to invoke it - the model is not the engine.

In that respect, it comes down to

How much of the game is dynamically generated using inference?
Where should that run ? 

The game runtime can be local or cloud. The model can be local or cloud. The architecture could be all local, all cloud, or hybrid

An all cloud game works, but might be laggy and expensive to host and maintain in terms of tokens and cloud compute

An all local game works but unless it is an extreeeeemely light game, you are trading token costs for cooking GPUs.

Hybrid makes the most sense, lightweight local inference model/component for low latency/high frequency things (dialogue etc, behavioural things) remote inference/cloud compute for anything heavy

Or just use AI to make and maintain the game - but not be the runtime (which is where we are at now)

And of course, use AI to churn out slop content for battlepasses 😆

replies.author: fatheadlifter
replies.body:
It may be hard to describe what I'm talking about just in words.  But I'm talking about AI being used as the renderer, the content generator, in realtime.

I'm well aware of what current limits are.  I'm steeped in both AI software and gamedev, I understand this is not the reality for gaming today.  I was talking about a future hypothetical, where we assume several of the shortcomings you point out are resolved or mitigated.

I'm talking about a hypothetical game that is both generative and locally run.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
Nope. Hardware is too expensive. You might be able to run one small model on the average person's PC that dynamically creates a single aspect of the game on a background thread. You're not getting an AI to create anything worthwhile dynamically that can simultaneously run on the average PC. Many users already struggle to just run a base game, they're not running a model demanding 20GB of VRAM simultaneously.

Talking hypotheticals beyond this are pointless.

Hell, forget 20GB of VRAM. You have to understand that the average Steam user's PC specs are fucking 16GB of SYSTEM RAM. SYSTEM RAM. And that's not improving anytime soon after the RAM price hikes. The average GPU has 8GB of VRAM and is a  3060/4060, neither of which can run any AI worth a damn.

The best you're getting here is a game that keeps its VRAM footprint between 3-4GB (so 2d or extremely low poly 3d without dynamic shadows, and a firm cap on textures/sprites), and then you could run a quantized tiny LLM (3B parameter or so Qwen model, NOT MOE since their system RAM is so limited.)

You can train that AI to do one thing well. One very limited thing.
